summaries.example: Imagine a magician writes down what side a coin will show before someone flips it. If the later flip somehow caused the earlier prediction, that would be backward causation. Philosophers ask whether this could really happen, or whether the prediction and the flip merely match by chance.
summaries.summary: Backward causation is the idea that a cause could happen later in time than its effect. This is difficult to imagine because everyday causes usually come first: a push happens before a toy moves, for example. The philosophical discussion asks whether time must always have this order, whether the past could be influenced without being changed into something different, and how we could tell causes from effects without simply looking at which came first. A famous challenge, called the bilking argument, says that once an earlier event has happened, we could try to prevent the later event that supposedly caused it. Other puzzles concern loops, choices, and whether a settled future leaves room for free will. Some physical theories describe basic processes as reversible in time, but the entry explains that this does not by itself prove that backward causation occurs. Different philosophical and physical interpretations remain under debate.
key_ideas: Usually, we think causes happen before their effects. Backward causation would reverse that usual time order.
Backward causation is not exactly the same as time travel. Time travel involves a traveler and often a loop; backward causation could be discussed without a traveler.
Some philosophers think the future must be real in a way similar to the past for backward causation to make sense.
The bilking argument says that after an earlier effect happens, someone might stop the later cause. Supporters of backward causation offer replies to this argument.
The topic connects ideas about time, causation, free choice, puzzles, and some interpretations of physics.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea helps us examine assumptions that often feel obvious: that causes must come first, that the future is not real yet, and that a free choice must be able to turn out differently. It also shows why unusual results in physics should not automatically be called proof that the future changes the past.

important_terms.definition: A possible connection in which a later event helps bring about an earlier event.
An event or action that helps make another event happen.
An event that happens because of another event.
The idea that only what is happening now is fully real; the past is gone and the future is not here yet.
The view that past, present, and future events all exist in some sense.
A puzzle that seems to produce a contradiction or impossible result.

questions_to_think_about: If a later event matched an earlier event, how could we tell whether it caused it?
Would a real future have to exist for it to affect the past?
Could someone freely choose if the future were already a fact?
Is every strange time story a case of backward causation?

summaries.example: Suppose a highly accurate predictor announces tomorrow’s coin toss today. After hearing the announcement, an experimenter tries to prevent the predicted toss or arrange the opposite result. The bilking argument claims that this intervention would show that the later toss could not have caused the earlier announcement. A defender might reply that the intervention changes the situation, or that the attempted prevention could itself be part of a consistent pattern. The example therefore raises questions about intervention, information, semantic content, and what counts as a causal relation.
summaries.summary:
Backward causation, also called retrocausation, is the thesis that an event can be causally prior to another event even when it occurs later in time. The thesis challenges the familiar assumption that temporal precedence defines the direction of causation. It must be distinguished from time travel: time travel involves a causal loop, while backward causation need not involve closed time-like paths or a traveler.

Several philosophical issues follow. A theory that treats the future as unreal may have difficulty explaining how a future event could cause a present or past event, whereas eternalism treats past, present, and future events as equally real. Yet eternalism does not imply that the future is causally determined by the past. It distinguishes a future that is already determinate from one fixed by earlier conditions or laws. This distinction matters to debates about free will.

The bilking argument claims that once an alleged effect has occurred, an agent could intervene and prevent the later cause. If the cause can be prevented, it seems unable to have caused the effect. Responses question whether the intervention is genuinely possible, whether it changes the relevant circumstances, and whether the argument confuses particular events with general causal patterns. The entry also examines whether causal direction can be explained through counterfactuals, probabilities, interventions, information, or physical quantities.

Paradoxes include causal loops, consistency problems, and Newcomb’s problem. Physics adds further complications: fundamental laws may be time-reversal invariant even though ordinary macroscopic processes are effectively irreversible. key_ideas: Backward causation requires separating temporal order from causal order. A cause might be later than its effect without simply changing an already completed past.
The view is distinct from time travel. Time travel involves a causal loop, whereas backward causation need not involve a traveler or a closed time-like path.

Presentism and a growing-block view make backward causation difficult to formulate because the future is not yet real. Eternalism supplies future events as truth-makers, but accepting eternalism does not by itself establish backward causation.

Counterfactual theories of causation face difficulties. In ordinary cases, both a cause and an effect may counterfactually depend on one another, and standard methods for evaluating counterfactuals can mishandle backward-looking cases.

The bilking argument challenges backward causation through intervention. Replies include distinguishing event-types from particular events, denying that intervention is always possible, or arguing that the intervention changes the causal circumstances.
Paradoxes include causal loops, consistency problems involving attempts to alter the past, and Newcomb’s problem, which connects prediction, choice, and the status of the future.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue tests whether our ordinary idea of causation depends on the direction of time or on deeper features such as intervention, counterfactual dependence, probability, and physical laws. It also clarifies why time-symmetric equations or quantum correlations do not automatically establish that the future causes the past. Studying the dispute is a useful lesson in separating logical possibility, metaphysical interpretation, and empirical evidence.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that a later event can be causally prior to an earlier event, even though it is temporally later.
A relation in which one event brings about, influences, or makes another event occur; some theories define it using probabilities, interventions, or counterfactuals.
A statement about what would happen under a supposition, such as “If c had not occurred, e would not have occurred.”
The argument that, after an alleged effect occurs, an agent could intervene to prevent its alleged cause, apparently showing that the cause was not genuinely causally independent.
The view that past, present, and future events all exist tenselessly, rather than coming into existence one after another.
A view on which only present events exist; the past no longer exists and the future does not yet exist.
A causal loop in which a chain of events eventually returns to an earlier event, so that an event appears to depend on what it itself helps cause.
A distinction between a future fixed by earlier laws and conditions, and a future that is already a definite fact even if it was not causally fixed by the present.

questions_to_think_about: Can a causal relation be defined without referring to which event happened first?
Does being a definite future fact make an action unfree, or does freedom require only that the action was not causally forced?
Would preventing an alleged cause after its effect show that backward causation is impossible, or only that this particular causal process did not occur?
Are quantum correlations evidence for backward causation, or can they be explained through non-separability without communication into the past?
What would count as empirical evidence for backward causation rather than an unusual correlation?

summaries.example: A fortune teller predicts that Maya will choose one box tomorrow. Before Maya chooses, a helper secretly puts a large prize in the box only when the prediction is that Maya will choose it alone. Maya knows the fortune teller has always been right. One argument says she should choose both boxes because the prize is already there. Another says she should choose only the special box because the prediction has always matched the choice. The puzzle does not prove backward causation, but it shows how prediction, time, choice, and causation can pull our reasoning in different directions.
summaries.summary:
Backward causation is the possibility that an event occurring later in time causes or influences an event that occurred earlier. This conflicts with ordinary experience, where a spark starts a fire and the fire comes afterward. The philosophical question is whether “earlier than” is part of the meaning of “cause,” or whether causation might have another direction that does not simply follow the clock.

The idea is not identical to time travel. Time travel involves a system moving through time while keeping its own time order, and it can produce a causal loop. Backward causation, by contrast, could be a relation between events without a traveler or a closed loop. Supporters also distinguish influencing the past from changing it: the past need not become different from what it was; rather, the later event may be part of why the past turned out as it did.

Theories of time affect the debate. Presentism says only the present exists, and the growing-block view adds the past but not the future. Eternalism says all times exist. Since a future cause would need to exist in some sense, backward causation appears to fit most naturally with eternalism. Critics worry that this makes the future fixed and threatens free will. A response distinguishes determinateness—there being a fact about what will happen—from determination by earlier causes or laws.

The bilking argument is a central challenge. If a later event caused an earlier one, then after the earlier event happened, someone might prevent the later event. This seems to show that the later event was not its cause. Replies question whether the intervention is possible, whether it changes the relevant conditions, and whether the argument concerns types of events rather than the same particular event. key_ideas: Our usual picture says a cause comes earlier than its effect, but backward causation asks whether that order is necessary or only common.
Backward causation and time travel are related but different. Time travel involves a causal loop; backward causation might occur without a traveler going around a loop.
Different views of time matter. Presentism says only the present exists, while eternalism treats all times as real. Backward causation seems easier to describe on the eternalist view.
A later event might influence the past without making the past different from what it was. The past could have included that influence all along.
The bilking argument uses the possibility of intervention to challenge backward causation, but philosophers disagree about whether the intervention would really be possible or decisive.
Questions about free will depend on a difference between a future that is already determinate and a future that is causally forced by earlier events.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic teaches us to separate several ideas that are often blended together: time travel, causation, prediction, determinism, and free will. It also shows how a philosophical possibility can be discussed without claiming that it occurs in our world. In physics, time-symmetric laws and quantum correlations may motivate interpretations involving backward influence, but the entry presents these as disputed possibilities rather than settled facts.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a later event can help cause an earlier event, instead of causes always coming first in time.
The event that produces, influences, or helps bring about another event.
The event produced or influenced by a cause.
The view that past and present events exist, while future events are not yet real.
The view that past, present, and future events all exist as parts of one complete temporal structure.
A reasoning test that asks what would happen if something had not occurred.
A challenge claiming that, after an effect occurs, one could stop its supposed later cause, making the causal claim look inconsistent.
A puzzling causal circle in which events depend on one another in a loop.

questions_to_think_about: If the future is real, does that mean it is already forced?
Can an event influence the past without changing the past?
Would stopping a supposed cause prove that it never caused the earlier event?
How might a causal loop be different from ordinary time travel?
Why might a physics experiment that looks backward in time have another explanation?
